lead: A three-phase voltage-source inverter (VSI) has three legs and six switches across a DC bus. Each leg connects its output to either the positive or the negative rail. In 180° conduction every switch stays on for 180°, so three switches — one in each leg — are on at every instant. The line-to-line voltage becomes a six-step wave. In 120° conduction each switch stays on for 120°, only two switches are on, and each leg has two 60° dead intervals, 120° in total. Motor drives, UPS units and solar inverters use this bridge.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for the single-phase bridge and its square wave.

sections.h3: Three legs and the 180° switch table

blocks.text: Label the six switches S1 to S6. Leg A uses S1 (top) and S4 (bottom); leg B uses S3 (top) and S6 (bottom); leg C uses S5 (top) and S2 (bottom). V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage in volts. In 180° mode each gate pulse is 180° wide and the pulses are spaced by 60°. The two switches in one leg are complementary: S1 on means S4 off, so the leg never connects both rails together.

At any instant exactly three switches are on, one per leg. From 0° to 60°, S1, S5 and S6 conduct. Phases A and C are tied to the positive rail through S1 and S5, and phase B is tied to the negative rail through S6, so current flows from the positive rail through A and C and returns through B. The table lists the active switches for each 60° interval. The pattern repeats every 360°. The output period is 1/f, where f is the output frequency in hertz.

Take the midpoint of the DC bus as the reference. A phase terminal sits at +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 when its top switch is on and at −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 when its bottom switch is on. The phase-to-neutral voltage is not a two-level square wave: it steps among +V<sub>dc</sub>/3, +2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and −2V<sub>dc</sub>/3. The line-to-line voltage has only three levels: +V<sub>dc</sub>, 0 and −V<sub>dc</sub>. It changes every 60°, which gives the name six-step inverter. The same bridge with 180° pulses is also called a square-wave VSI.

V<sub>LL(rms)</sub> = √(2/3) V<sub>dc</sub> ≈ 0.816 V<sub>dc</sub>; V<sub>ph(rms)</sub> = V<sub>LL(rms)</sub>/√3 ≈ 0.471 V<sub>dc</sub>; V<sub>LL1(rms)</sub> = (√6/π) V<sub>dc</sub> ≈ 0.780 V<sub>dc</sub>; V<sub>ph1(rms)</sub> = (√2/π) V<sub>dc</sub> ≈ 0.450 V<sub>dc</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage in volts; V<sub>LL(rms)</sub> is the total rms line-to-line voltage; V<sub>ph(rms)</sub> is the total rms phase-to-neutral voltage; V<sub>LL1</sub> and V<sub>ph1</sub> are fundamental rms values.

blocks.text: The total rms is larger than the fundamental because the six-step wave contains 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th and higher harmonics. The fundamental produces positive torque in a motor; the harmonics heat the motor and cause torque ripple. Voltage control methods change the fundamental without changing Vdc; see Chapter 4.3.

In 120° mode each gate pulse is only 120° wide. At any instant two switches conduct, not three. Each device conducts for 120°, which is one third of the cycle. Each leg has two 60° intervals — 120° in total per cycle — in which both of its switches are off. For example, the top device conducts from 0° to 120° and the bottom device from 180° to 300°, so that leg is off from 120° to 180° and again from 300° to 360°. Because the gate pattern itself leaves two 60° dead intervals in every leg, an overlap fault is much less likely than in 180° mode.

The penalty is a more distorted output: each device conducts for only one third of the cycle, the line-to-line voltage steps through +V<sub>dc</sub>, +V<sub>dc</sub>/2, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and −V<sub>dc</sub>, and the fundamental is lower than in 180° mode (about 0.39 V<sub>dc</sub> phase rms, 0.68 V<sub>dc</sub> line rms). With an inductive load the phase current freewheels through the freewheeling diode of that leg, which clamps the terminal to the positive or the negative rail depending on the current direction; no switch of that leg is on. With a purely resistive load the current is simply zero and the terminal floats to the neutral potential. The bridge is still a square-wave VSI, but it is less common because switch utilisation is poorer.

The name conduction angle means the angle for which one switch is on in one cycle. It is not the firing delay angle of a thyristor rectifier. A 180° switch conducts half the cycle; a 120° switch conducts one third.

figure.caption: Gate signals over one 360° cycle in 180° mode: every switch conducts for 180°, pulses are 60° apart, and exactly three switches are on at any instant.

spec.aria: Six gate signals over one 360° cycle: each device conducts 180°, and at every instant exactly three devices, one per leg, are on.

examples.question: A three-phase bridge in 180° mode has V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V and feeds a star-connected load of 10 Ω per phase. Find the rms line-to-line voltage, the rms phase voltage, the total power and the fundamental phase voltage rms.
examples.answer: Line rms is 326.6 V, phase rms is 188.6 V, total power is 10.7 kW (10666.7 W), and fundamental phase rms is 180.0 V.
examples.check:
import math
Vdc = 400
R = 10
Vll = math.sqrt(2/3) * Vdc
Vph = Vll / math.sqrt(3)
P = 3 * Vph**2 / R
V1 = math.sqrt(2) / math.pi * Vdc
print(f"{Vll:.1f}")
print(f"{Vph:.1f}")
print(f"{P:.1f}")
print(f"{V1:.1f}")

traps: Reading 180° mode as 'both switches of a leg on together' — it means each device conducts 180°, and the two devices of a leg stay complementary.
Mixing phase and line rms values. In 180° mode the line rms is 0.816 V<sub>dc</sub> and the phase rms is 0.471 V<sub>dc</sub>.
Calling the conduction angle a firing angle. 180° or 120° is the switch on-time, not a thyristor delay angle.
Forgetting that the total rms line voltage includes harmonics. The fundamental is 0.78 V<sub>dc</sub>, which is lower than 0.816 V<sub>dc</sub>.
Thinking 120° mode has three devices on. It has only two, and each leg has two 60° gaps (120° in total per cycle), so the gate pattern itself keeps a leg from shorting the DC bus.

quiz.q: In 180° conduction, how many switches conduct at any instant?
quiz.a: Three switches conduct, one in each leg.

quiz.q: Why is an overlap fault much less likely in 120° mode than in 180° mode?
quiz.a: Each leg has two 60° gaps, 120° in total per cycle, with both switches off; the upper and lower switch of one leg are never on together in the gate pattern.

quiz.q: A 180° mode VSI has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V. Find the rms line-to-line voltage and the rms phase voltage.
Why is the fundamental line rms 0.78 V<sub>dc</sub> smaller than the total rms line voltage 0.816 V<sub>dc</sub>?
quiz.a: The total rms includes the fundamental plus 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th and higher harmonics; the fundamental is only the first component.

quiz.q: Give two other names for a three-phase VSI operated in 180° mode.
List the phase-to-neutral voltage levels in 180° mode.
In 120° mode with a star load, what carries the load current during a leg's 60° gap?
quiz.a: With an inductive load the phase current freewheels through the freewheeling diode of that leg, which clamps the terminal to the positive or the negative rail depending on the current direction; no switch of that leg is on. With a purely resistive load the current is zero and the terminal floats to the neutral potential.

quiz.q: For 180° mode and V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V, find the fundamental phase voltage rms.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the six-step VSI is the starting point for variable-frequency drives, where a rectifier front end and a DC link feed the bridge. Traction inverters use PWM instead, but the same three-leg bridge remains. Search next for '180-degree conduction three-phase inverter', 'six-step voltage source inverter' and 'three-phase VSI switch states'. Modern drives add dead time, current sensing and field-oriented control around this bridge.
